Circles And Parallelogram

CirclesGeometryConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: two circles meet a second time on the diagonal of a slanted four-sided box.
How to play: Drag the points A, B, C, D, M, N and K, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show point names, the line between the circle centres, or the hint.
Look for the math

Drag K along MN and watch the two circles: their second meeting point P slides along the diagonal AC. Two other things do not change at all — the slant of the line joining the centres, and its length.

The second meeting point

Start with a parallelogram ABCD, a point M on AB and a point N on CD. Put K anywhere on MN. Draw the circumcircle of triangle AMK and the circumcircle of triangle CNK. Besides K they meet once more, at P. The page claims that P always lies on the diagonal AC, and the logic test checks this for more than two thousand drawings: the signed area of triangle ACP is zero every time.

Why the angle stays put

Because A, M, K and P lie on one circle, the angles at P and at M in that four-point ring add to 180° (an inscribed quadrilateral). Since P is on AC, the angle between KP and the diagonal is just the angle at P. The angle at M is the angle between MA and MK: MA lies along the side AB, and MK lies along MN, so it depends on the parallelogram and on MN, but not on where K sits. The page says the angle KP makes with AC is independent of K, and the test confirms it: sliding K through many positions changes that angle by less than a billionth of a degree.

The line between the centres

Both circle centres are the same distance from K and from P, so they lie on the perpendicular bisector of the common chord KP. Each centre also lies on the perpendicular bisector of its own fixed chord, AM or CN. As K slides, those two fixed lines do not move, so the centres slide along them in step: the line joining them keeps the same direction and the same length. Tick “Hint” to see the bisectors and the chord KP; tick “Centre line” to see the pair of centres.

When the circles touch

Move K to where MN crosses AC. The two circles then have only one common point, K = P, and their common tangent there makes the same angle with AC as the chord KP did just before the two points merged. The test checks this limit on nearly a hundred parallelograms, comparing the tangent angle with the chord angle a little way along MN.

Try this: tick both “Hint” and “Centre line”, then drag K slowly towards the diagonal. Watch KP turn into the short line through K where the two circles touch, while the dashed line between the centres keeps its slant.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
